djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.title: Resettlement for the Ambouli dike at Djibouti city
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.place: Ambouli wadi and the PK 12 resettlement site, Djibouti city, Djibouti
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.point: Ambouli, Djibouti city, on the wadi where the flood protection dike was rebuilt. The resettlement site is at PK 12, about 12 km out of the city. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Ambouli, Djibouti.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Flood Emergency Rehabilitation Project (P089968). Credit 3977-DJ and Grant H123-DJ, SDR 2.2 million credit and SDR 3.6 million grant, approved by the Board on 2 September 2004; the financing agreement and the project agreement were signed on 2 October 2004. Additional financing of SDR 1.4 million approved by the Board in February 2007 (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 October 2009). The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 May 2010 rates it Moderately Unsatisfactory. Both rate the risk to the development outcome Significant. The completion report rates Bank performance Satisfactory; the review rates it Moderately Satisfactory. Both rate borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Agence Djiboutienne d'Execution des Travaux d'Interet Public (ADETIP)
companies.role: Government contract-management agency that ran the works and the resettlement site. In 2007 Parliament widened its mandate to the National Initiative for Human Development and it was renamed Agence Djiboutienne de Developpement Social (ADDS), into which ADETIP was folded. It did not report the jobs its labour-intensive works were meant to create.

companies.name: Housing Fund of the Ministry of Urban Development, Djibouti
companies.role: State fund that built the 277 dwellings at PK 12, called Cite Gargaar, and sold them to the resettled families on hire-purchase terms. It also produced the report on the resettled families' situation after the study the project had planned was dropped.

djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.community: Floods on 13 April 2004 killed an estimated 100 people in Djibouti city and affected more than 100,000. The project rebuilt the Ambouli embankment dike and paid for basic services at a resettlement site 12 km out of the city, called PK 12. The completion report's indicator table says 100 per cent of families were resettled, and that this takes in "approx. 240 families affected by the flood and 120 affected by the dike construction and resettled later on". The report's account of the Bank's internal quality review puts it the same way: compensation for "some 120 families living on the reconstruction site, as well as another 240 families who were victims of the flood" had to be settled before the dike could be designed and tendered. The government's own completion report, printed inside the same document, gives different figures. It says the rehousing plan "involves 127 households, of whom 55 are victims of the flooding and 72 have been displaced by the dike reconstruction work". The Bank's text also says that out of 127 families eligible for resettlement at PK 12, 94 took a new house, 2 took a plot and the rest moved elsewhere. In the project's first year the government did not hand occupancy permits to the families moved to PK 12, did not provide their precise numbers or names, and postponed dealing with compensation; the permits were a condition of the credit for delivering latrines and water at the site. The resettlement plan the government filed in July 2006 does carry a named list, of 127 households living in 105 structures affected by the dike construction, with a cut-off date of 2 June 2005. The Bank's team recorded that the government was reluctant to apply the resettlement policy, which it considered too generous towards illegal squatters. At PK 12 the report says the new houses are better than those the flood destroyed and that water standpipes and latrines were provided, but that the families "have difficulty finding jobs, as the resettlement site is far from downtown Djibouti", and that several of the resettled families had made a living from vegetable gardening in the Ambouli river bed. At the last supervision meeting the residents said water supply had failed for the previous two months and that schools and work were far away. The report answers that the distance to the city centre is real but that no land was available for resettlement closer in. It says the resettlement action plan was in the end prepared and implemented in a satisfactory manner, and the evaluation review says all 360 families were given occupancy permits.
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.displaced_label: families moved off the dike reconstruction site, from the World Bank's completion report, which gives the figure as approximate
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 660 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. Four counts sit in the record and do not reconcile. The completion report's indicator table gives about 120 families affected by the dike construction and resettled later on, and about 240 moved because of the flood, 360 in all; its account of the Bank's internal quality review gives the same 120 as families living on the reconstruction site. The same report's own narrative says 127 families were eligible for resettlement at PK 12, of whom 94 took a house and 2 a plot, which cannot be squared with 360. The government's report, printed inside the completion report, gives 127 households in all, of whom 55 are flood victims and 72 displaced by the dike reconstruction work; that passage is written in the future tense and describes the plan rather than the result. The resettlement plan of 15 July 2006 covers the transfer of 127 households living in 105 structures, all of them for the dike construction. The figure held here is the completion report's 120, the only count the report attaches both to the dike works and to a word meaning moved.
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.killed_note: The April 2004 floods killed an estimated 100 people, before the credit was approved. The completion report records no death caused by the project's works.
djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.outcome: The dike was finished in March 2009, after the closing date had been pushed back from 30 September 2008. The completion report says some works to ease the flow of water in the river were still unfinished, partly because people had moved into the area, and that the government had not stopped people settling in the river bed and banks or dumping trash there. Financing was secured for an upstream dam at Boulle to take pressure off the dike. Of the 400 latrines planned for PK 12, 300 were built; the report says that number is sufficient for the resettled population.

sources.title: Djibouti - Flood Emergency Rehabilitation Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Djibouti - Flood Emergency Rehabilitation: ICR Review (Independent Evaluation Group)
Projet de reconstruction suite aux inondations : l'etat des lieux

djibouti-ambouli-dike-resettlement.confidence_note: The relocation counts and the problems at PK 12 come only from the World Bank's own completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The Djiboutian agency that ran the works has published a short notice confirming the project and the conditions set for the dike, but no figures for the resettlement and no account of what the families lost. No independent press report, court record or audit of the PK 12 resettlement was found. The two counts of families moved for the dike, about 120 and 72, sit in the same document and are not reconciled.

kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.title: Land taken for Kigali electricity lines before a resettlement plan existed
kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.point: Kimihurura, Gasabo District, Kigali, one of the sectors the retrospective resettlement plan lists by name. The works ran along distribution line routes and four mini substation sites across the district. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Kimihurura, Kigali, Rwanda.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Urgent Electricity Rehabilitation Project (P090194), Credit 4032-RW, US$25 million, approved 27 January 2005, Credit Agreement dated 23 February 2005. The completion report of 1 August 2011 rates the outcome Satisfactory and the risk to the development outcome Low or Negligible; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 22 March 2012 rates the outcome Satisfactory and the risk Negligible to Low.

companies.name: Electrogaz
companies.role: Rwanda's state electricity and water utility at the time, which carried out the works through a project coordination unit housed inside it and reporting to a steering committee headed by the Ministry of Infrastructure. The utility's survey team, with the project unit's safeguards adviser, drew up the inventory of land and crops along the routes.

kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.community: The project rebuilt electricity distribution networks in Kigali, in Gasabo District. Under the lender's own rules a resettlement action plan has to be written before works that take land begin, and no civil works are to start until the people affected have been compensated. For the Gasabo distribution lines and four mini substations, the plan was written afterwards. The document is titled "Retrospective Resettlement Action Plan", is dated June 2010, and says plainly: "the report has been prepared after compensation has occurred". Civil works began in November 2007. The plan gives 2.5741 hectares of land to be acquired and 440 people affected by the loss of land, structures, crops or trees, 95 of them through land expropriation. It says there was "already some compensation in form of cash provided to the PAPs following displacement that has occurred". Its own payment annexes show money still owed. For land the grand total is RWF 122,145,102, of which RWF 109,785,402 is marked paid and RWF 12,359,700 "not yet paid". For structures, crops and trees the total to be paid is RWF 94,574,341, of which RWF 88,285,300 is marked paid and RWF 6,289,041 "not yet paid". The same document also states that works began only after all affected people had been identified and compensation provided, and that copies of the cheques can be produced on request. A separate abbreviated plan for the Birembo substation at Kinyinya, in the same district and dated July 2008, records four affected people and says the land acquisition "will lead to the physical displacement of some of the households living in the project site". It names one of them, a widow who it says demolished her mud-walled house and moved to a rented house nearby before compensation reached her, and states that she alone of the four would be given funds to build a new house, the other three being landlords who had rented their dwellings out. The completion report says resettlement and compensation of project-affected people "was completed satisfactorily". The evaluation review carries the same sentence but attributes it to the Bank's project team rather than to a document.
kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 459 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The retrospective plan counts 440 people affected by the loss of land, structures, crops or trees, in the future tense, and no document counts anyone rehoused. The abbreviated plan for the Birembo substation, dated July 2008, says the land acquisition there will physically displace some of the households on the site and names four affected people without counting anyone moved. The abbreviated plan for the Jabana thermal power plant, of the same month, is the one that says its land acquisition would cause economic and not physical displacement.
kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.outcome: The project closed in 2011 and the completion report rates it Satisfactory. The retrospective plan's annexes leave RWF 18,648,741 of compensation marked as not yet paid as of June 2010, across the two payment tables. No later document in the project's record says whether that money was paid.

kigali-gasabo-electricity-land-retrospec.confidence_note: The unpaid amounts and the fact that the plan was written after the works come from the plan the government itself filed with the lender in June 2010, and from the lender's completion report. That is the strongest part of the record, because it is the borrower's own admission. The same document contradicts itself: one passage says all affected people were compensated before works began, and its annexes show money not yet paid. The named widow at the Birembo substation comes from the borrower's own abbreviated plan of July 2008, which is a plan and not an outcome document. No independent press report, court record or audit of these payments was found.

rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.title: Relocations and two deaths at Rwanda's hillside irrigation dams
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.place: Nyanza 23 dam site, Nyanza District, Southern Province, Rwanda
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.point: Nyanza District, Southern Province, where the Nyanza 23 dam was built. It is one of the project's six resettlement-plan sites; the 117 households moved are counted across all of them. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Nyanza, Southern Province, Rwanda.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Land Husbandry, Water Harvesting and Hillside Irrigation Project (P114931). Credit 4674-RW, approved 22 December 2009, Financing Agreement 8 February 2010; additional financing under Credit 5360-RW, Financing Agreement 30 December 2013. The completion report of 17 December 2018 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 3 May 2019 both rate the outcome Satisfactory; the review also rates Bank performance Satisfactory.

companies.name: Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources, Rwanda (MINAGRI)
companies.role: Ran the project through a Single Project Implementation Unit shared with the Rural Sector Support Project, which prepared the resettlement plans, paid compensation and set up 15 grievance committees. The ministry paid the burial costs for one of the two people who died.

rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.community: The project built irrigation dams, diversion weirs and hillside terraces at sites across Rwanda. The completion report counts 2,135 project-affected households, "of which 117 required relocation and were resettled in Project constructed houses". Compensation came to more than RWF 1.41 billion, about US$1.6 million, and 1,288 affected households were offered work during the terracing. The report says households were compensated under Rwanda's expropriation law of 11 June 2015, before civil works began, and that where that law and the lender's policy differed the lender's policy was applied. Two people died during the works. In July 2016 a contractor's worker fell into a spillway foundation pit; the report says that death "was noted as being the result of ineffective safety measures around excavated areas in the site". In November 2017 a boy drowned in a dam reservoir. The worker was insured and his family was paid by both the insurer and the contractor; the drowned boy's family was given money by the ministry for the burial. The project unit then ordered an environmental, health and safety audit of all its dam sites. Fifteen grievance committees recorded eight kinds of complaint. Four were claims against the project: disagreement over the value of resettlement or compensation between an affected person and the independent valuer; inactive or missing bank accounts that delayed compensation; missing land titles that delayed both compensation and construction; and erosion, runoff and dust away from the sites. Four were claims the project treated as unfounded or as matters between neighbours: people who claimed compensation without having been affected; people who claimed for assets acquired after the cut-off date; disputes between neighbours over adjoining plots; and successions, divorces and other family disputes over who owned an asset. The report says all grievances were resolved and that proper records of them are held. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats the 2,135 and 117 figures and says compensation and jobs were provided ahead of any civil works; it does not mention either death.
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.displaced_label: households relocated and resettled in project-built houses, from the World Bank's completion report
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 423 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 2,135 project-affected households, of which 117 were relocated. A resettlement plan for the Nyanza 23 dam, dated August 2012, had set out 124 households to be compensated without relocation and 20 to be compensated and relocated at that one site.
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.killed_note: Both deaths are recorded in the completion report with a cause. One was a contractor's worker who fell into a spillway foundation pit in July 2016, which the report attributes to ineffective safety measures around excavated areas at the site. The other was a boy who drowned in a dam reservoir in November 2017. The report calls them the project's two fatalities. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of the report does not mention them.
rwanda-hillside-irrigation-relocation-de.outcome: The project closed in 2018 and both the completion report and the evaluation review rate it Satisfactory. Dams were built at four sites, Nyanza 23, Kayonza 4, Rwamagana 34 and Muyanza, and the other sites used diversion weirs. The review records that only 66 per cent of farmers pay their water fees and that construction at the largest irrigation site was finished only in June 2018, at the end of the project.

No independent press report, court record, inquest or audit of the two deaths was found. The completion report does not say which of the four dam sites either death happened at, so the point on the map is one of the six resettlement-plan sites and not the site of the deaths.

kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.title: Fifty-seven households moved for the Mufuchani bridge at Kitwe
kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.point: Ipusukilo, Kitwe, the settlement the resettlement plan names as holding 55 of the 57 households whose homes stood in the bridge alignment. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Ipusukilo, Kitwe, Zambia.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Phase of the Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P106596), Credit IDA-46540, Credit Number 4654-ZA, approved 16 October 2009, agreement dated 25 November 2009. The completion report of 26 October 2016 rates safeguards compliance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 1 May 2017 repeats the completion report's account of the resettlement.

companies.name: Road Development Agency, Zambia
companies.role: The roads agency under the Ministry of Works and Supply that commissioned the bridge and prepared the Mufuchani Resettlement Action Plan of February 2009. Its Environmental and Social Management Unit, set up under the national road programme ROADSIP, monitored the works.

kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.community: The credit paid for a new bridge over the Kafue River at Mufuchani, to link the Mufuchani farming area to Kitwe. Before the bridge there was no motorised crossing; the nearest route was about 10 km away. The resettlement plan of February 2009 records 57 households whose homes stood fully in the way, 55 of them in the Ipusukilo Stage III settlement and 2 on the Mufuchani farming block, and three more properties partly affected, being two churches and one house. It counts 333 affected people, 27 landlords, 21 food stalls to be helped to move, 370 fruit trees, one farm plot of 248 square metres and two crop plots totalling 64 square metres. The completion report records what was built: "57 new houses, two churches, and a 1.5 km access road were constructed in Kitwe in the Copperbelt Province", with water, sewerage and electricity connected "to ensure smooth relocation of project affected people". The Times of Zambia, in a report published on 18 January 2014, described the handover the day before of 57 houses and two churches in the Kawama and Ipusukilo townships of Kitwe, at a cost of K17 million, built under the Mufuchani Resettlement Action Programme with World Bank funding, and quoted the works minister saying the government wanted to provide decent housing for the affected families. The completion report says the project complied with all safeguard policies and that no major environmental or social safeguards issue arose during it.
kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.displaced_label: households rehoused for the bridge alignment; the figure is the resettlement plan's count of households fully affected and matches the 57 houses the completion report records as built
kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 333 for this project. That is the resettlement plan's own count of project-affected persons at Mufuchani, not a count of people moved.
kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.outcome: The bridge was finished on 31 January 2016 and 371,570 vehicles a year crossed it, against a target of 60,000. The documents record no complaint from the households moved, and no later figure for what they lost. In January 2016 the Times of Zambia reported that Kitwe City Council had demolished the houses of more than 20 families in the Mufuchani settlement, saying their plots had been acquired illegally, and that the families were given offer letters for other plots across the Kafue River and put up at a hotel; the report does not connect those demolitions to the bridge resettlement.

kitwe-mufuchani-bridge-relocation.confidence_note: The relocation itself is corroborated outside the lender: the Times of Zambia reported the handover of 57 houses and two churches at Kawama and Ipusukilo in January 2014, with the cost and the minister who handed them over. What the households lost beyond their homes is not documented anywhere. The completion report says no major social safeguards issue arose, and no source records a complaint from the people moved. The later demolition of more than 20 houses in the Mufuchani settlement by Kitwe City Council, reported in January 2016, is not tied to this project by any source and is not counted here.

beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.title: Five deaths and a failed compensation process on Mozambique's urban climate works
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.place: Beira, Sofala Province, and the ravines 3 and 4 site in Maputo, Mozambique
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.point: Beira, Sofala Province, where the drainage and green urban infrastructure works ran and where all the recorded deaths happened. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Beira, Sofala, Mozambique.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Cities and Climate Change Project (P123201), Credit IDA-50660, US$120 million approved 3 April 2012; the Financing Agreement for Credit 5066-MZ is dated 2012, the day on its signature line being illegible in the disclosed text. The credit is SDR 78.2 million, US$120 million equivalent. Additional financing of US$15.75 million from the Strategic Climate Fund under the Pilot Program for Climate Resilience, made up of a US$6.5 million loan and a US$9.25 million grant, was approved by the Board on 23 October 2014 and declared effective on 7 April 2015. Actual disbursement US$122,517,360.69 in credit and US$15,561,840.66 in grants. Closed 30 September 2020, against an original closing date of 15 December 2017. The completion report of 30 March 2021 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 August 2021 both rate the outcome Satisfactory.

lenders.name: KfW (German Development Bank)
lenders.role: Parallel financing of EUR 18 million for the green urban infrastructure works on the Chiveve River in downtown Beira, alongside the Bank's additional financing. Those works ran past the Bank project's closing date, and the safeguards left unfinished at closing, including the return of market vendors, were handled under a post-closing plan the Bank monitored with KfW.

companies.name: Administracao de Infra-estruturas de Agua e Saneamento (AIAS)
companies.role: Mozambique's water and sanitation infrastructure administration, under the Ministry of Public Works, Housing and Water Resources. The project implementation unit for the drainage and green infrastructure works in Beira and Maputo sat inside it, and it was the body the Bank held to the resettlement and labour audits after closing.

beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.community: The project paid for drainage works in Beira and Maputo and for green urban infrastructure along the Chiveve River in central Beira. The completion report says the works in Beira "recorded recurrent issues of non-compliance with OHS and community health and safety plans" and names the deaths. For the Beira drainage works it counts "the fatality of one worker and three community members", and its footnote gives the causes: a worker hit by a third-party vehicle while moving between work sites; a nine-year-old child who drowned in the retention basin construction site outside working hours; and two people killed in traffic accidents involving the contractor's vehicles. For the green infrastructure works in Beira a second footnote records "a fatality of a 7-year old child who was hit by a contractor's vehicle". Those works' main difficulty, the report says, was the contractor's lack of commitment to community and worker safety and to national employment and labour law, including weekly rest and limits on working hours. The report also names two more deaths it does not attribute to the project: another child found dead in the drainage canals outside the construction sites, and a body found in the Chiveve retention basin during construction. In Beira the project built 21 new houses and 81 latrines for structures the works hit, paid for 498 trees, and compensated 610 people who grew vegetables in small plots known locally as machambas, reaching 98 per cent of them for their crops. In Maputo the report says resettlement "was problematic". The canal's original line would have affected seven houses at a site known as ravines 3 and 4. By the time the plan was being written the number of affected people had risen to 18, and they had already left the land after being paid by a private developer who was buying the land rights from the Municipality of Maputo. The Bank's team could not get clear information from the agency or the municipality and demanded an independent audit. The audit found the money the developer paid "did not meet the requirements of Bank safeguard policies and was not developed in accordance with the applicable Mozambican legislation". It told the project to give a new plot to one affected person who had wanted to be compensated by the municipality instead, to provide land papers to the others, to help those who had lost their source of income, and to pay six months of lost income. The audit was presented in February 2018 and the project reported the fixes done in June 2018, before the works started.
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.displaced_label: people who had left the ravines 3 and 4 site in Maputo, from the Independent Evaluation Group's review, which says the project-affected people, 18 in total, had already received compensation from a private developer and resettled; the money that moved them came from that developer, which was buying the land rights from the municipality, and not from the credit
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 276 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report says the canal's original line would have affected seven houses and that by the time the plan was prepared the number of affected people had risen to 18; the evaluation review calls the 18 a total of people. In Beira the project built 21 houses for structures the works hit and temporarily moved market vendors, and the documents give no count of the vendors.
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.killed_note: Five deaths in Beira are recorded with a cause tied to the works or the contractor: a worker hit by a third-party vehicle while moving between work sites, a nine-year-old child who drowned in the retention basin construction site, two people killed in traffic accidents involving the contractor's vehicles, and a seven-year-old child hit by a contractor's vehicle on the green infrastructure works. The documents do not agree on the total. The Independent Evaluation Group's review gives four fatalities, one worker and three community members, and leaves out the seven-year-old. A lessons paragraph in the completion report itself says four fatalities of community members were caused by traffic accidents involving construction vehicles, where its own footnotes give three. Two further deaths are named and are not counted here: another child found dead in the drainage canals outside the construction sites, and a body found in the Chiveve retention basin during construction, which the report says was not shown to be related to the works.
beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2020, almost three years late. The safeguards rating on the municipal grant component fell to Moderately Unsatisfactory in 2016, after a review found that 20 municipalities lacked the capacity to run environmental and social measures on small works, and was back at Moderately Satisfactory by closing. A labour audit finished in October 2020 and an environmental audit in November 2020; by mid-March 2021 the contractor had not produced satisfactory evidence for 11 of the labour audit's corrective actions, 15 per cent of them, and 14 of the environmental audit's measures, 21 per cent, were late. The updated plan for putting market vendors back into the new Chiveve market had been sent to the Bank but could only be carried out after the works were handed to the agency and the municipality in late March or early April 2021, a handover delayed by Cyclone Eloise. The green infrastructure works also had direct impacts on protected mangroves in the Chiveve basin, and restoring them was part of the post-closing plan.

beira-maputo-climate-works-deaths-compen.confidence_note: The deaths and the audit finding come only from the World Bank's completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of that report. The audit that found the compensation unlawful was commissioned by the Bank's own team, so it is not independent of the lender. The count of deaths differs between the two documents and within the completion report itself, and both versions are given above.

lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.title: Farmland taken and two households moved for Lesotho's road works
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.place: Nyenye to Makhoroana road, Leribe District, Lesotho
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.point: Ha-Nyenye, Leribe District, at one end of the Nyenye to Makhoroana road the additional financing scaled up. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Nyenye, Lesotho.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Lesotho Integrated Transport Project (P075566), Credit IDA-42370 approved 19 October 2006, with later IDA-48270, grants IDA H-2550 and IDA H-6230 and trust fund TF-90728; the Financing Agreement for Credit 4827-LS and Grant H623-LS is dated 9 October 2010. The completion report of 21 December 2015 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2016 both rate the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The review rates the quality of supervision Moderately Unsatisfactory. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Ministry of Public Works and Transport, Lesotho
companies.role: Ran the project through a project implementation unit with posts for an environment and social coordinator, a resettlement desk and an HIV/AIDS coordinator. Both of the unit's safeguards specialists left in the project's second year and were not replaced for the additional financing, and no safeguards specialist joined the lender's own supervision missions for that stage.

lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.community: The credit paid for road works in Lesotho, including two bridges over the Senqu and Senqunyane rivers and work on two junction roads, Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng and Nyenye to Makhoroana. Floods in March 2011 damaged both roads so badly that the planned resealing had to become full rehabilitation; there was not enough credit for all 64 km, so the lender paid for the first 20 km of the Nyenye to Makhoroana road and the government undertook to cover the remaining 17 km and the Teyateyaneng to Mapoteng road. The completion report says the first assessment found resettlement "confined to two households", but that compensation also had to be paid for many strips of farmland where the road was widened for bus and taxi stops. When the additional financing was added, the report says, the assessment of its safeguards impacts was underestimated and implementation was unsatisfactory: environmental measures were neither systematically monitored nor documented, workers' safety measures "were only respected partially", and further resettlement activities were found later. New culverts, added when the road design changed, "induced adverse impacts on farmland", and the mission that wrote the report saw stones and loose material fallen onto the roads in many places. A small number of temporary market stalls were moved to make room for the works at Makhoroana. A new taxi rank was being built on land the local chief gave, and the report's authors objected that the taxi association had still not been formally engaged. No resettlement completion report was prepared. The Independent Evaluation Group's review repeats these findings and says that "it is not clear from the ICR whether the resettlement activities were complete at project closure". The report also records that prostitutes went to the construction camp, that condoms were often not available there because of its remote location, and that a social impacts study at completion found HIV infection rates had risen; the implementing agency denies that less attention was given to this under the additional financing.
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.displaced_label: households resettled, from the World Bank's completion report, which calls this the initial assessment and says further resettlement activities were identified later
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 247 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report's only count of households resettled is two. It gives no number for the strips of farmland compensated, for the stalls moved, or for the resettlement activities found later.
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.killed_note: The completion report discusses road deaths in Lesotho as a policy problem, at around 15 deaths per 100,000 people a year, and records no death caused by the project's works.
lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.outcome: The project closed in 2015. The completion report rates safeguards performance moderately unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group says the report's account of safeguards compliance is unclear and that it cannot be told from it whether the project complied at closing. No resettlement completion report was produced, so there is no record of what the affected farmers were finally paid.

sources.title: Lesotho - Integrated Transport Project: Implementation Completion and Results Report
Lesotho - Integrated Transport Project: ICR Review (Independent Evaluation Group)

lesotho-integrated-transport-farmland-an.confidence_note: Everything here comes from the World Bank's completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. The harm is real but small and poorly counted: two households resettled, an unnumbered set of farmland strips, and culverts that damaged farmland without any figure for the area or the farmers. No resettlement completion report exists, and the evaluation review says it cannot be told from the completion report whether the resettlement was finished. No Lesotho press report, court record or audit of these payments was found.

rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.title: Thirty households moved and compensation delayed on Rwanda's electricity rollout
rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.place: Rukarara substation site, Nyamagabe District, Southern Province, Rwanda
rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.point: Nyamagabe District, Southern Province, where the Rukarara substation stands. The evaluation review names it as the one sub-project that took land and moved people; the distribution lines that took no land ran across the country. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Nyamagabe District, Rwanda.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Rwanda Electricity Access Scale-up and Sector Wide Approach Development Project (P111567), Credits IDA-46510 and IDA-51930, approved 15 October 2009, with additional financing under P126483 and P126489. Original commitment US$70 million, revised to US$130 million, actual US$124,496,525.55. Original closing date 31 January 2014; actual closing 30 March 2018. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 20 March 2019 rates the outcome Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory.

lenders.name: OPEC Fund for International Development
lenders.role: Funded the Rukarara substation sub-project, the one sub-project within the sector-wide programme that took land and moved people, according to the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 20 March 2019.

companies.name: Energy Water and Sanitation Authority, Rwanda
companies.role: The state utility that carried out the electricity access programme, through the project implementation unit the evaluation review names as the body that prepared the consolidated report on the eight sub-project environmental and social management plans and the resettlement completion report.

rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.community: The project was a sector-wide programme to extend electricity to households and public institutions in Rwanda, with the lender's credit alongside money from other funders under one set of safeguards rules. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says that one sub-project, the Rukarara substation funded by the OPEC Fund, "involved land acquisition and physical relocation", and that the other sub-projects, which were distribution lines, took no land and so involved only compensation for trees and crops. "In total, 3,678 households were affected, including 75 households that lost land and 30 households that were physically relocated." The review then names the main problem: "The key challenge in the implementation of the RAPs was the delays in compensation because of unavailability of the required cash on time." All compensation payments were finished by the end of December 2017, nine years after the project was approved. The project prepared a resettlement completion report and sent it to the Bank; the review says that report shows the project was always in full compliance with resettlement guidelines during implementation.
rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.displaced_label: households physically relocated, from the Independent Evaluation Group's review of the completion report, which attributes the figure to the completion report at page 38
rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 234 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The evaluation review counts 3,678 affected households, of which 75 lost land and 30 were physically relocated. The review says the one sub-project that took land and moved people was the Rukarara substation, funded by the OPEC Fund rather than by the Bank's credit.
rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.outcome: The project closed on 30 March 2018, more than four years after its original closing date. Compensation payments were completed by the end of December 2017. The Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Satisfactory. Its review is the only outcome document reached for this project: the completion report itself is cited in it by page but is not in the project's disclosed document list.

sources.title: Rwanda - Rwanda Electricity Access Scale-up Project: ICR Review (Independent Evaluation Group)

rwanda-electricity-access-rukarara-reloc.confidence_note: This rests on a single document, the Independent Evaluation Group's review of a completion report that was not reached, so every figure here is the review quoting that report at page 38. The relocation it counts happened at the Rukarara substation, which the review says the OPEC Fund paid for with a parallel loan of US$10 million; that sub-project sits inside the component the lender appraised and is covered by the project's own resettlement policy framework, which is why it is on this card, but the credit did not pay for it. The compensation delays the review names fall on the distribution lines the credit did finance, and the review gives no count of how many households were paid late. No Rwandan press report, court record or audit of these payments was found.

sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.title: Right-of-way clearance, 13,600 job losses and a mine death on the Sena railway
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.place: Sena railway line, Dondo to Moatize, Mozambique
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.point: Dondo, Sofala Province, the southern end of the Sena line that the project rebuilt. The households moved were spread along the line, for which the documents give no separate locations. Coordinate from OpenStreetMap's Nominatim search for Dondo, Sofala, Mozambique.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Beira Railway Project (P082618), Credit 3991-MOZ, US$110 million, approved 14 October 2004, Development Credit Agreement and project agreements with the concession company and the state ports and railways enterprise all dated 16 December 2004. The completion report of 27 June 2012 rates the outcome Unsatisfactory and Bank performance Unsatisfactory; it gives the risk to the development outcome as Significant in its risk assessment section and as Substantial in its summary data sheet, and the two are not reconciled. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 6 November 2013 rates the outcome Unsatisfactory, the risk High and both Bank and borrower performance Unsatisfactory, where the completion report rated borrower performance Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Companhia dos Caminhos de Ferro da Beira (CCFB)
companies.role: The concession company that held the Beira railway system. The appraisal document records its shares split 51 per cent to the concessionaire consortium and 49 per cent to the state railway and ports enterprise, which the completion report says left the public side with little or no leverage over major decisions.

companies.name: RITES Limited
companies.role: Indian state railway consultancy. With Ircon International it formed the consortium awarded the Beira railway concession on 30 August 2004 after international competitive bidding, holding 51 per cent of the concession company; the two also set up the joint venture RICON to manage the project. Railway Gazette reported in February 2007 that the pair were rebuilding the line under a US$175 million concession awarded in 2004.

companies.name: Ircon International Limited
companies.role: Indian state railway construction company, the other half of the concessionaire consortium holding 51 per cent of the concession company and a partner in the RICON joint venture that managed the works.

companies.name: Portos e Caminhos de Ferro de Mocambique, E.P. (CFM)
companies.role: Mozambique's state ports and railways enterprise, which held 49 per cent of the concession company while also supervising the project for the government. The completion report says this blurred whether it was regulator, policy maker, client or operator, and that its 49 per cent stake biased its supervision. It carried out the resettlement and the environmental clean-up, and it and the independent engineer intervened several times on safety, as far as expelling managers, stopping work and closing workers' camps.

sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.community: The credit paid for rebuilding the Sena railway line between Dondo and Moatize, closed since 1983 and booby-trapped with landmines during the war. The completion report puts the rehabilitation component at 600 km and describes the line de-mined as 671 km. The line had to be cleared of mines, within 15 metres each side, before work could start; clearance of the whole line finished in October 2006, and de-mining teams went back out whenever contractors found residual mines. The completion report says: "Sadly, one worker was killed by these residual mines. Five more were killed in rail accidents." On people moved, the report records that "Thirty-seven households, five businesses and five religious facilities were relocated to make way for a 50m right of way on each side of the line", and that all the individuals and businesses were compensated. It also records that 13,600 staff, all of them employees of the state ports and railways enterprise, were retrenched as a precondition of the concession, that they were retrained, and that around 6,000 found work in new trades. On safety the report says occupational health and safety compliance "had not been addressed", that "Health and Safety at work standards at all sites were extremely low and the work conditions were often hazardous", and that construction waste and unrestored borrow pits were still outstanding at the final mission in December 2011. It says there was a visible and documented lack of concern for health and safety by the consortium, that the state enterprise and the independent engineer intervened several times, to the point of expelling managers, stopping work and closing workers' camps, and that those records could have been the base for more stringent action by the Bank, or for forcing cancellation of contracts with contravening contractors, but that this was never done; the Independent Evaluation Group repeats the passage. Both documents say compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy was reported as satisfactory or highly satisfactory throughout.
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.displaced_label: households relocated for the 50-metre right of way each side of the line, from the World Bank's completion report, which also counts five businesses and five religious facilities
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 190 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The completion report counts 37 households, five businesses and five religious facilities relocated.
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.killed_note: The completion report records one worker killed by a residual landmine during the de-mining the project required, and says five more people were killed in rail accidents. It does not say who those five were, when they died or whether they were workers, passengers or people at level crossings, so they are not counted. Mozambique's war left the line mined; the mines were not laid by the project, but the clearance work that killed the worker was the project's own.
sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.outcome: The concession was terminated at the end of 2011 and the government took the rail system back. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group also rates Bank performance Unsatisfactory, saying design and supervision both fell short. Of the 13,600 retrenched staff, the report says around 6,000 found work in new trades; it gives no figure for the rest. Railway Gazette reported in February 2007 that services on the southern section were to resume before March that year, with the concessionaires hoping to finish the whole 670 km network by May 2009.

sena-railway-right-of-way-and-retrenchme.confidence_note: The relocations, the retrenchments and the mine death come only from the World Bank's completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it. Railway Gazette corroborates the concession, the two Indian state companies that held it and the rebuilding timetable, but reports nothing about people moved, jobs lost or deaths. No Mozambican press report, court record or audit of the right-of-way clearance or the retrenchment was found. The report's five rail-accident deaths are left uncounted because it says nothing about who died or when.

fields_add.community: On the Ethiopian side the completion report records a fatal accident: a local employee died when a company vehicle he was driving was swept away during heavy floods. Ethiopian Electric Power gave the financiers a detailed report on the death, with an assessment of safeguards and health and safety compliance, which the completion report says the financiers deemed satisfactory. On the Kenyan side the same report records a fatal accident in February 2017 involving a contractor's employee under Lot 4, without giving a cause; the utility shared the full report with the financiers and the Bank judged health and safety compliance satisfactory. The livestock feed processing plant built for those who lost the grazing land was completed only after protracted delays, with the affected people then organising themselves into a cooperative to run it. As part of livelihood restoration in Ethiopia, 25 settlements holding more than 3,000 households were given mini-grid electricity under the project. Theft of materials from the transmission towers led to heavier surveillance and a redesign of the towers with a barrier to make them harder to climb.

tanzania-central-transport-corridor-road.drop_reason: No relocation count and no unmet loss, on the project's own documents. The Project Performance Assessment Report of 21 June 2011 is a joint report covering five projects in Tanzania and Uganda, and this project, Credit 3888-TA, is Annex B. Annex B's safeguards section, paragraph 18, says the project was category A, that full environmental and social assessments were done at preparation, and that "The Involuntary Resettlement Policy (OP 4.12) was triggered for Zanzibar because of land purchases and a resettlement framework and RAPs for roads were implemented based on procedures and guidelines outlined in the governing policies. All compensation claims and grievances were settled. Some 870 persons were affected at a cost of TZS 250 million." Annex B paragraph 19 covers the railway: a resettlement plan was prepared "since 145 project-affected people were identified living near the rail right-of-way who could be affected due to increased train speeds. Since the reverse happened, and train speeds fell due to the deteriorating condition of the railways, the risk did not materialize, and the RAP was never implemented." So nobody was moved for the railway either. Annex B also records, in its borrower performance section, that the railway operator was responsible for the environmental cleaning and for implementing the resettlement plan and that "There were delays in these activities due to the retrenchment of staff, but a consultant was employed to assist with completing the work"; no document says who was affected by that delay or for how long. The completion report of 29 June 2010 was read for the outcome and agrees: its paragraph 45 gives Table 1, counting 870 persons affected on three Zanzibar road sections, 174 on residential houses and 696 on commercial properties, and Table 2 showing actual compensation of TZS 250.20 million paid, under the sentence "All compensation claims and grievances were settled accordingly based on the monitoring and evaluation plan." Its paragraph 46 gives the same account of the unimplemented railway plan. What remains is a count of people affected with compensation paid in full and no count of anyone relocated, which the forward rule treats as a drop. Two candidate sentences offered for this row came from the wrong half of the joint assessment report and are not evidence about this project: "For those components that were completed there was no relocation of households" and "About 1,000 people were displaced and a further 25,000 adversely affected by the severe floods" both sit in Annex A, which evaluates Tanzania's Second Integrated Roads Project, Credit 2598-TA, and its El Nino flood rehabilitation component. Neither was used.

mozambique-transfrontier-conservation-to.drop_reason: The resettlement in this project's area was paid for by another lender and the credit financed none of it. The completion report of 30 December 2014 says in its footnote 1: "Involuntary resettlement within the targeted TFCAs was not an objective of the TFCATDP, and no project funding was allocated to resettlement activities. However, the World Bank agreed to provide advisory services to involuntary resettlement activities funded by the KfW in Limpopo National Park, but outside of TFCATDP implementation and Bank supervision." The same footnote says the implementation of both resettlement plans "faced some issues", blaming the government's lack of knowledge and commitment, KfW's lack of knowledge of resettlement safeguards and insufficient budget, and the Bank's lack of a local social scientist. The outcome document was read for a relocation count and holds none. Its Table 10, which looks like one, is the opposite: the number of families living inside three parks fell from 2,050 to 448, and paragraph 38 explains that this was done by moving the park boundaries, "excising (i.e. re-demarcation) the more densely populated areas so that fewer people would have to be resettled". The evaluation review of 23 November 2015 adds nothing on resettlement beyond naming the policy. ICIJ's 691 for this row is the figure in the April 2008 resettlement plan for Macavene village, which states that "the population of Macavene is 691 people in 128 household units" and plans to move those 128 households to Banga and Tihovene; it is a plan census, not an outcome. A Mail and Guardian report of 6 April 2018 describes about 2,000 families resettled from eight villages in the Massingir area, with no farming land, no jobs and water now bought rather than drawn, but names no funder, so it cannot be tied to this credit.

greater-maputo-water-supply-expansion.drop_reason: A count of affected people with compensation paid, and no relocation. The completion report of 25 February 2022 says at paragraph 64 that for the transmission main between Corumana and Machava "The RAP was successfully implemented, as the 387 affected people were adequately compensated, and the 93 claims received were properly addressed." The outcome document's own Annex 5 was also read: its paragraph 6 says a full resettlement plan was prepared and implemented for the 94 km of transmission main from Corumana Dam to the Machava Distribution Centre and that "A total of 393 PAPs were identified and adequately compensated" — 393 against the 387 in paragraph 64, unreconciled in the same report. Annex 5 paragraph 7 says the post-resettlement evaluation found that affected people received appropriate compensation and were able to restore their livelihoods where applicable, and paragraph 3 says no severe or permanently disabling health and safety incident was reported on any contract and no deaths. The route was densely populated, mostly street vendors and public utilities, and the report says all grievances and complaints were adequately and timely resolved. No document counts anyone relocated and none records an unpaid or short payment.

kenya-energy-sector-recovery-lavington.drop_reason: No documented loss to identifiable people. The completion report of 27 March 2014 was read for the outcome. Its resettlement bullet says the plan's provisions were invoked only for the 66 kV line from Nairobi North Substation to Westlands, that from August 2011 the utility "paid compensation to 113 eligible owners of structures/houses along the right of way for this transmission line, in accordance with the RAP", and that the affected people who lost land, crops, trees, structures or dwellings "were satisfied with the RAP implementation and payments", witnessed by the chief of the Karura location whose office verified ownership and kept the census list. The one disputed strand is the Lavington substation in Nairobi, and it did not turn on a recorded loss. The Inspection Panel's own case page for case 79 records a Request received 10 May 2012 from Mr Peter Usher on behalf of the Njumbi Road Residents' Association, alleging the substation development was "illegal, inappropriate, environmentally unsound and poses a danger to people living near the development" — an anticipated danger. The Panel registered the Request on 24 May 2012 and did not recommend an investigation, publishing its eligibility report on 25 July 2012 and saying the legitimacy of the siting process was outside its purview and before the National Environment Tribunal. The completion report records the Tribunal's ruling of 1 March 2013 cancelling the environmental licence of 24 February 2011 and revoking the approval of 30 December 2010, and directing the utility to relocate the substation; the utility appealed to the High Court on 2 April 2013 and the substation was left incomplete. No document records a death, injury, arrest, unpaid compensation or lost livelihood. The completion report's monitoring table also carries a row for "Evictions of Maasai communities in the Lake Navaisha area", and its own entry states the evictions "are related neither to KenGen nor to the Olkaria II project", with no count and no date, so nothing can be built on it.

ethiopia-urban-water-supply-sanitation.drop_reason: The harm the outcome document records is real but names nobody and nowhere. The completion report of 29 June 2018 says at paragraph 83 that "The project complied with all applicable environmental and social safeguards", and then: "However, in some project locations, there were delays due to lack of capacity for undertaking necessary assessments and using necessary tools; delays related to compensation and resettlement for project-affected people (PAPs); lack of sufficient attention and compensation for livelihoods-related losses; lack of safeguards experts in secondary cities (early in the project); poor documentation for safeguards in some cities; and late implementation of grievance redress systems that were recommended to be strengthened with limited progress." It does not say which of the cities — Addis Ababa, Gondar, Hawassa, Jimma, Mekelle and Dire Dawa — nor how many people, nor what the livelihood losses were. The only count in the outcome document is paragraph 84: "A total of 89 project affected persons were compensated, following the RAPs." The resettlement plan of October 2014 for the Kaliti wastewater treatment plant and sewer lines in Addis Ababa plans for 269 affected households, of which "31 households will lose their residential housing units resulting in relocation" and 238 would lose part of a housing unit, a fence or similar; those are plan figures and no outcome document carries them or any other relocation count. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 September 2018 drops the shortcomings altogether and says only that "All 89 project affected people were compensated following the RAPs". This is the closest call in the batch: the completion report does record compensation delays and under-compensated livelihood losses, which is limb (b) language, but with no place, no count and no identifiable people it cannot be written as a card without inventing the missing parts.

mauritius-infrastructure-project-b6-road.drop_reason: Land taken, compensation paid in full before the works, and no relocation. The completion report of 25 June 2015 was read for the outcome. Its paragraph 50 says involuntary resettlement was triggered because upgrading the B6 Belle Rive to Quartier Militaire road required land acquisition and compensation, that an abbreviated resettlement plan — called a Land Acquisition Plan in Mauritius — was prepared, disclosed before appraisal and "implemented in a manner satisfactory to the Bank before the commencement of respective works", under almost bi-monthly supervision, and that "The compensation for the land acquisition was paid by the GoM's own resources in the amount of US$1.1 million", held in a separate escrow account at the Ministry of Housing and Lands. The report's paragraph 40 records that the mid-term review of February 2013 found "the progress of compensation for the land acquisition for the B6 works was slow and posed a risk that the compensation process would not be completed before completion of the upgrading of the road", and states that all the review's issues "were addressed and resolved by the project closing". No document counts affected people or households, none counts anyone relocated, and none records a payment unmade or below replacement cost.
